assessment.rationale: This simulation is largely orthogonal to the scenario. It proposes a CAS object typing pattern (broad codec plus deterministic internal kind), which may help payload auditability and evolution, but it does not model ring forwarding, per-hop authorization, refusal recording, hop skipping, or membership reconfiguration. As a PromiseGrid component idea it is plausible and fairly durable, but as evidence for this transport authorization-failure bakeoff it is a weak fit.
strengths: Internal kind can improve fine-grained local dispatch and auditability.
Plausible evolution path within a broad object family.
weaknesses: Does not address per-hop authorization failure behavior.
No ring, gossip, relay, or membership semantics are specified.
Promise vocabulary is not actor/payload-promise-first and remains design-level.
risks: The design provides no explicit failure semantics for unauthorized forwarding, so scenario pressure is unanswered.
Using both codec and internal kind risks creating two competing type authorities.
Transport designers may overgeneralize payload typing benefits into transport-layer suitability without evidence.
open_questions: Can this typing scheme express transport-hop authorization refusals at all, or is it entirely orthogonal to the scenario?
If both codec and internal kind influence dispatch, which one is authoritative when they conflict?
Would a transport protocol need separate refusal-record objects beyond this CAS typing mechanism?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
